label: Chapter 7 · Part A
title: Common Objections I: “What Caused God?” and Other Misfires
tagline: Why the most popular objections miss the arguments they aim at
oneSentence: The best-known objections to First Cause arguments — “What caused God?”, “Maybe the universe is the uncaused cause”, “Why assume a beginning?”, “fallacy of composition”, “god of the gaps”, “a universe from nothing” — fail because they attack a caricature no major defender ever held, ignore the principled reasons the real arguments give, or quietly beg the question, so a serious critic has to engage the actual premises instead.
bigPicture:
After five proofs (chapters 1–5) and a long derivation of the divine attributes (chapter 6), Feser turns to the objections people actually raise. He has answered most of them already along the way, but he thinks a separate chapter is warranted for two reasons: there are some objections he has not yet addressed, and some of the weakest objections are so widespread — and so loudly repeated by the “New Atheist” writers (Dawkins, Dennett, Harris, Hitchens, Stenger, Krauss, Rosenberg, Grayling, Hawking and Mlodinow) — that they deserve a fresh, deeper look. This module covers the first half of that chapter: the objections aimed mainly at First Cause (cosmological) reasoning.

The unifying diagnosis is that almost every popular objection **misfires**: it is aimed at an argument nobody in the tradition ever gave. The flagship example is “If everything has a cause, then what caused God?” — an objection that presupposes the proofs start from the premise that *everything* has a cause, which none of them does. Feser devotes several pages to the history of this caricature, following the Thomist W. Norris Clarke in tracing it through Russell and the Mills back to Hume, who seems to have confused the rationalists’ talk of everything having a *sufficient reason* with the claim that everything has an *efficient cause distinct from itself*.

The remaining objections fall into recognizable families. Some nominate a rival stopping point (the universe, the Big Bang, the multiverse, quantum events, the laws of physics) while ignoring the criterion each proof uses to decide what can and cannot be a stopping point. Some deny that causal or explanatory principles hold universally, but rely on confusions (chance and indeterminism are not uncausedness) or on bad inferences (what we can *conceive* apart is not thereby *possible* apart). Some assume a temporal beginning or a linear series when the proofs concern a hierarchical, here-and-now series. Some misread technical terms — “necessary” as “true by definition”, “nothing” as a kind of exotic stuff. Some are true but irrelevant (the proofs don’t establish the Trinity). And the “god of the gaps” charge — which Feser calls the central conceit of the New Atheism — treats a metaphysical demonstration as if it were a rival scientific hypothesis.

This module matters enormously for the learner’s third goal, persuasion. In real conversations you will hear these objections far more often than any sophisticated criticism. Knowing *why* each one misfires, and being able to say so in a calm sentence or two, lets you redirect the conversation to where the genuine debate lies: whether the premises of the proofs — about act and potency, composition, essence and existence, and contingency — are true.
objectives: Explain the two independent reasons “If everything has a cause, what caused God?” fails: none of the proofs assumes everything has a cause, and each proof gives a principled reason why the First Cause could not have a cause.

Reconstruct W. Norris Clarke’s account of how the “everything has a cause” caricature entered the literature (Hume, the Mills, Russell, Hospers) through a confusion of efficient cause with sufficient reason.

Use each proof’s own criterion (potentiality, composition, essence–existence distinction, contingency) to show why the universe, Big Bang, multiverse, quantum events, or laws of physics cannot be the ultimate uncaused cause — and why the attempt would yield pantheism rather than atheism.
Distinguish chance and quantum indeterminism from uncausedness, and state three problems with Hume’s claim that we can conceive of an effect without a cause.
Explain why the proofs do not need a beginning of the universe, and why an endless stack of deeper physical laws would itself be a hierarchical series needing a first member.
Turn the fallacy-of-composition charge back on Hume and Grayling using the sticks, the mirrors, and Leibniz’s geometry books.
Distinguish logical, merely conditional, and metaphysical necessity, and use the distinction to rebut Kant’s and Grayling’s claim that the cosmological argument presupposes the ontological argument.
Explain why the proofs are not “god of the gaps” reasoning, and why Krauss’s and Hawking–Mlodinow’s “universe from nothing” never actually starts from nothing.
Give a calm, one-sentence reply to each objection and then redirect the conversation to the real premises.

summary.heading: Why a chapter on objections at all
summary.body:
Feser opens by admitting some overlap with earlier chapters, where most objections were already answered in context. Two things justify a separate treatment. First, there are further objections not yet discussed. Second, certain objections, though very weak on close inspection, are so common and reveal such widespread misunderstanding of the arguments that they deserve revisiting — especially since the New Atheist books (Harris, Dawkins, Dennett, Hitchens, Stenger, Hawking and Mlodinow, Krauss, Rosenberg, Grayling) have given them fresh publicity. He promises to come at the familiar objections from new angles and in more depth rather than simply repeating himself.

The chapter is organized as a series of headings, each one an objection stated in the objector’s own voice, followed by Feser’s reply. This module covers the first run of them — those aimed chiefly at First Cause reasoning.

summary.heading: “If everything has a cause, what caused God?” — two fatal problems
summary.body:
Feser calls this perhaps the single most common objection to arguments for a divine cause, raised by amateurs and professionals alike and repeated throughout New Atheist literature (Dawkins, Dennett, Harris, Hawking and Mlodinow, Hitchens, Krauss, Stenger).

**Problem one: a straw man.** None of the book’s arguments has “everything has a cause” as a premise. So the charge that the theist contradicts himself, or makes an arbitrary exception for God, attacks a position nobody holds.

**Problem two: the arguments explain *why* God has no cause.** Even apart from the straw man, the arguments don’t just stipulate that God is uncaused. Part of their whole point is to show that there must be something that not only happens to lack a cause but *could not* have one, because it lacks the very feature that makes other things need causes:

- **Aristotelian proof:** things need a cause because they mix actuality and potentiality, and a potential cannot actualize itself. What is *purely actual* has no potential to be actualized.
- **Neo-Platonic proof:** composite things need a cause to account for the combining of their parts. What is *absolutely simple* has no parts to combine.
- **Thomistic proof:** a thing is kept in existence by having existence joined to its essence, which requires a cause. What *is* existence itself has nothing to be joined.
- **Rationalist proof:** contingent things need a cause because they could have been otherwise. A *necessary* being could not have been otherwise.

(A footnote sets the Augustinian proof aside: it is not a causal argument, so the objection isn’t even superficially relevant to it.)

Read in light of what the arguments mean by “cause” and “God”, the question becomes “What caused the thing that could not in principle have a cause?” — What actualized the potentials of that which has none? What assembled the parts of that which has no parts? What joined the essence and existence of that in which they are not distinct? What gave a reason for existence to that which has its reason within itself? None of these questions makes sense.

Feser grants that an atheist may doubt that the arguments really establish such a being, or may try to show that pure actuality, simplicity, and the rest are secretly incoherent. That would be a real objection. But simply asking “What caused God?”, as though defenders had overlooked the most obvious point imaginable, misses the whole argument. A serious critic has to deal with the details rather than trying to dispose of them with one smug question. The objection also fails against other historical versions of the cosmological argument, for mostly the same reason.

summary.heading: The straw man everyone attacks: the “basic cosmological argument”
summary.body:
Why, then, is such a poor objection so popular? Largely because critics nearly always target a straw-man version of the argument that is widely assumed to capture its basic thrust. Feser gives examples from very different kinds of writers:

- **Dennett** (New Atheist) summarizes the argument’s “simplest form” as: since everything must have a cause, the universe must have a cause, namely God.
- **Nigel Warburton** (popular introduction to philosophy) says the argument claims that absolutely everything was caused by something prior, and that following the chain back gets you to a very first cause.
- **Graham Priest** (a rigorous logician, not a philosopher of religion) motivates it from everyday cases — people don’t fall ill for no reason; cars don’t break down without a fault — so everything has a cause, and the cause of everything must be metaphysical: God.
- **Robin Le Poidevin** (a philosopher of religion) states a three-premise “basic cosmological argument”: whatever exists has a cause; nothing causes itself; the universe exists; so the universe has a cause outside itself.

The standard next step is predictable: “Then what caused God? And if nothing did, why not say nothing caused the universe?” Critics add that the argument gratuitously assumes a beginning of the universe, and they treat more sophisticated versions as desperate patches on this “basic” argument.

The trouble, Feser insists, is that **not one major defender of the cosmological argument ever gave this argument** — not Plato, Aristotle, Plotinus, al-Ghazali, Avicenna, Averroes, Maimonides, Anselm, Bonaventure, Aquinas, Scotus, Suárez, Leibniz, Clarke, Locke, Berkeley, nor modern defenders such as Garrigou-Lagrange, Maritain, Gilson, Adler, Reichenbach, Taylor, Swinburne, Koons, Gale, Pruss, Haldane, Martin, Oderberg, or Craig. Le Poidevin himself concedes that “no-one has defended a cosmological argument of precisely this form,” but still offers it as a useful stepping-stone.

Feser’s analogy: imagine Intelligent Design theorists defining “the basic Darwinian thesis” as the claim that a monkey once gave birth to a human baby, citing no Darwinian who ever said so, admitting nobody holds it, yet calling it a useful stepping-stone to the sophisticated versions. Darwinians would rightly be outraged, because the framing makes everything they say look like a salvage operation on an absurd idea. That is exactly the impression the “basic cosmological argument” creates.

Nor can defenders be said to be *implicitly* committed to the basic argument. None appeals to “everything has a cause”; some explicitly or implicitly deny it. None of those listed simply *assumes* the universe had a beginning; only one version (the kalām argument) even tries to *prove* it did. And most versions don’t argue from any premise about the universe as a whole.

summary.heading: How the caricature spread: the Hume–Russell tradition
summary.body:
If the straw man explains the popularity of the objection, what explains the popularity of the straw man? Part of the answer is that critics rely on other critics rather than reading Aquinas, Leibniz, and the rest — or they read the caricature into those authors. Repeated generation after generation, the caricature hardened into conventional wisdom, until even a specialist like Le Poidevin feels entitled to begin with it.

Feser then follows the diagnosis given by the Thomist **W. Norris Clarke** in a 1970 article on a “curious blind spot” in Anglo-American antitheistic argument. Clarke documented mid-twentieth-century textbooks presenting the caricature — including John Hospers’ widely used *An Introduction to Philosophical Analysis* — and suggested that Bertrand Russell’s *Why I Am Not a Christian* (a 1927 lecture reprinted in a 1957 book) taught it to many later writers. Russell seems to have got it from John Stuart Mill, who got it from his father James Mill; and David Hume, in his *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion*, may be the first famous writer to attack something like it.

Clarke’s key observations, in paraphrase: if anyone really held that every being has a cause, the refutation would indeed be crushing — but the very ease of the refutation should have made critics suspicious; and, tellingly, none of the writers in this tradition ever quotes an actual theistic philosopher who uses the principle.

Hospers, having accused First Cause arguers of contradicting themselves, remarked condescendingly that “many people” reach God by the argument and then forget the argument. Feser asks who these people are — we are never told — and turns the remark around: it is the *critics* who, having reached the destination they wanted (a way to dismiss Aristotle, Aquinas, and Leibniz wholesale), forget what those thinkers actually said. Clarke’s verdict is that this tradition started off by misrepresenting its target and has kept repeating itself, talking only to itself, never checking whether its opponent exists — a tradition in a rut.

summary.heading: Where the confusion began: Descartes, Spinoza, and two senses of “cause”
summary.body:
How did the tradition start? Clarke’s answer: Hume was reacting to what he *mistakenly* took Descartes and Spinoza to be saying.

In the Third Meditation Descartes offered an unusual variant of the First Cause argument (sometimes called the “preservation” argument), which implies that in some sense everything has a cause. But even this is not the straw man. Descartes isn’t asking what caused the universe; he asks what preserves *him* in existence from moment to moment. “Everything has a cause” does not appear as an explicit premise. And he makes no exception for God, since he regards God as *self-caused*. So even Descartes escapes “What caused God?” — he doesn’t deny that God has a “cause” in his sense.

Moreover, Clarke shows that Descartes, despite his confusing replies to critics, really means something close to the **principle of sufficient reason** (defended in chapter 5): everything has an *explanation*. That is not the same as saying everything has a cause in the sense of something that actualizes a potential; all causes are explanations, but not all explanations are causes. PSR-based arguments make no exception for God: contingent things are explained by something outside them, a necessary being by its own nature. Whatever one thinks of such arguments, they involve no inconsistency and no ad hoc exception.

Descartes and Spinoza (who also called God self-caused) blurred cause and sufficient reason. Because they used the word “cause”, they sounded as if they meant an **efficient cause distinct from its effect** — exactly the kind of cause God is traditionally said not to have, and which they themselves would deny God has. Hume, on Clarke’s reading, fused the two senses: he took the rationalist claim that everything has a cause-*as-sufficient-reason* to be the claim that everything has an efficient cause *distinct from itself*, and then attributed that claim to cosmological arguers generally. Since those arguers do deny that God has a distinct efficient cause, a contradiction appeared to follow. Clarke’s memorable verdict is that the target is a metaphysical monster, but “a monster of their own fabrication” — a hybrid of Scholastic and Cartesian ideas that would make sense in neither tradition and that both would reject.

Hume had some excuse given Descartes’ muddled terminology; his successors, with modern scholarship at their disposal, have much less. Feser proposes that willingness to accept Clarke’s judgment is a good test of the competence and intellectual honesty of anyone who comments on First Cause arguments. He adds that the complaint is old: in 1889 another Thomist, **Richard F. Clarke**, protested that the law of causation does *not* say everything that exists has a cause (God being uncaused), and that stating it that way misrepresents the theist’s position. Feser predicts the complaint will need repeating in another eighty years, because habits are hard to break — especially when breaking them means admitting that one’s side has rested its main objection on an elementary mistake for centuries.

summary.heading: “Maybe the universe (or the Big Bang, the multiverse, quantum events, the laws of physics) is the uncaused cause”
summary.body:
This objection also goes back at least to Hume, and appears in Dawkins, Dennett, Grayling, Krauss, Rosenberg, and Stenger. It too misses the point. There is no special pleading in saying that God needs no cause while everything else does, because each argument supplies a *principle* for the difference — and that same principle explains why the universe cannot be the terminus.

- **Aristotelian:** anything whose potentials are actualized needs a cause; only the purely actual does not. The universe mixes act and potency; the Big Bang was an actualization of potential; so would each stage of a multiverse be, and each quantum event (whether or not it is deterministic is beside the point). The laws of physics are merely potential too, since they could have been otherwise.
- **Neo-Platonic:** the universe and any multiverse are composite. Quantum events and physical laws lack the absolute simplicity the first principle must have; their very contingency shows a distinction between what they are and that they are.
- **Thomistic:** only something whose essence *is* existence can be the uncaused cause; none of these candidates qualifies.
- **Rationalist:** all of them are contingent, not necessary, and so cannot be the ultimate explanation.

**A closer look at “the laws of physics.”** The metaphysical status of laws is so contested that a casual appeal to them settles nothing. Feser lays out the options. If a law is just a *statement that a regularity exists*, it describes what needs explaining rather than explaining it. If a law is a kind of *Platonic entity*, we need an account of how the world comes to participate in it, and why in these laws rather than others — so laws aren’t ultimate. If a law is *shorthand for how substances naturally tend to behave* (the Aristotelian view, defended by David Oderberg), then laws depend on the substances and again can’t be ultimate.

The atheist may reject all of this, but that requires argument. Merely *suggesting* that the universe might be the stopping point is not a reason to reject the proofs — it simply ignores them.

**Even success would not yield atheism.** If the universe really were uncaused, self-explanatory, and necessary, it would possess distinctively divine attributes. The result would be *pantheism*: God exists and is identical with the world. Many Hindus could accept that; Jews, Christians, and Muslims could not — and neither could atheists.

summary.heading: “Not everything has a cause or an explanation”: chance and quantum mechanics
summary.body:
Stenger ascribes some events to “chance” rather than causation; Dennett and Rosenberg say quantum mechanics shows events can occur without a cause; Grayling repeats Hume’s claim that we can conceive of effects apart from causes. Setting aside (again) that the proofs don’t rest on “everything has a cause”, none of these touches even the causal principles the proofs *do* use.

**Chance.** Stenger’s point attacks a straw man: no defender of the argument denies that chance events happen. But chance doesn’t exclude causality — it *presupposes* non-chance causal regularities. The classic example: a farmer plowing a field strikes buried treasure. That is chance, but it happens only because two non-chance causal lines intersect — his decision to plow that direction that day and someone else’s decision to bury treasure in that spot. Likewise, it is chance that a boulder tumbling after an earthquake smashed *this particular* boulder, but that happens only because of regularities such as plate tectonics, gravity, and the solidity of rock.

**Quantum mechanics.** At most, quantum physics shows that some events lack a *deterministic* cause or explanation. Neither the principle of causality nor PSR demands determinism. Furthermore, quantum events occur, even indeterministically, only given the laws of quantum mechanics, which are contingent and merely potential until a universe governed by them is actualized. So appealing to quantum mechanics either misses the point or begs the question, since quantum reality is itself part of what the cosmological argument says needs explaining.

summary.heading: The Humean objection and three reasons it fails
summary.body:
Grayling treats Hume’s old point — that we can conceive of an effect without its cause — as a definitive reply to cosmological arguments. Feser gives three reasons it is nothing of the kind.

1. **Special pleading, and an explanation already on the table.** No working physicist, chemist, biologist, or neuroscientist would take seriously the suggestion that some phenomenon they are investigating might simply have no cause or explanation. The critic owes us a reason why that suggestion becomes respectable only when God is at issue. And as Lloyd Gerson notes, the cosmological argument *is itself* a proposed explanation — so it is no answer to say “maybe there’s no explanation in this case.” One has been offered; the critic needs some reason to reject it other than the bare possibility that there isn’t one.
2. **Conceivability doesn’t show possibility.** From “we can conceive of effects without causes” it does not follow that an event could actually occur uncaused. We can think of what a triangle is without thinking of it as three-sided (trilateral), yet no triangle could fail to be trilateral. We can think of a man without thinking of his height, yet no man could exist with no height at all.
3. **Anscombe’s point: the scenario is underdescribed.** Hume imagines an object popping into being out of nowhere. But what makes that a case of something coming into being *without a cause*, rather than coming into being with an *unseen* cause, or being transported from elsewhere by some unusual means (teleportation, say)? To make the imagined scene do Hume’s work, we must add something — yet it is hard to see what we could add that doesn’t bring causation back. For example, the natural way to distinguish *coming into being* from *being transported* is by reference to a *generating* rather than a *transporting* cause.

Feser notes that he treated the Humean objection and the quantum objection at more length in earlier chapters.

summary.heading: “Why assume the universe had a beginning, or that the regress must end?”
summary.body:
Rosenberg and Krauss suggest that the multiverse hypothesis — on which our Big Bang branched off from a preexisting universe within a beginningless series of universes — removes the need for a divine cause. Krauss, invoking Richard Feynman, also suggests there might be ever-deeper layers of physical law that we could keep probing until we got bored.

Feser’s replies:

- **The beginning is irrelevant.** As he has stressed repeatedly, the book’s arguments aren’t about whether the universe began. They argue that even a beginningless universe — or multiverse — would need a divine cause to *keep it in existence* continuously and to explain *why it exists at all*, beginning or no beginning.
- **Laws can’t be ultimate, however many layers.** The earlier point about laws applies to every layer.
- **Layers of laws would form a hierarchical series.** Laws at one level would hold only as a special case of laws at a deeper level, which hold only as a special case of deeper ones still. That is precisely the kind of per se (hierarchical) series described in chapter 1 — and such a series cannot lack a first member in the sense of something that imparts causal power without deriving it. Nothing Krauss or the other New Atheists say even addresses this, let alone refutes it.

summary.heading: “First Cause arguments commit a fallacy of composition”
summary.body:
Feser first notes that the arguments of this book don’t need any premise about the universe as a whole, so there is no part-to-whole inference to criticize. And chapter 5 showed that the part-to-whole reasoning that one version of the rationalist proof might use (inferring that the whole collection of contingent things is contingent) does not commit the fallacy.

Grayling, following Hume, says such arguments wrongly assume that once each member of a collection has been explained individually, something is left over — the collection as a whole — still needing explanation. Feser answers with three examples:

- **The sticks** (from chapter 1): even an infinite series of sticks each moving the next would need a mover outside the series, since no stick — individually or collectively — has the power to move anything on its own.
- **The mirrors**: even an infinite series of mirrors each reflecting a face from the next would need an actual face outside the series, since no mirror — individually or collectively — can generate the image by itself.
- **Leibniz’s geometry books**: if a geometry textbook was copied from an earlier copy, that one from a still earlier copy, and so on infinitely, we would still not know why the series exists with *this* content rather than some other. Tracing the causes back forever leaves the most important fact untouched.

The sticks and mirrors illustrate hierarchical series; Leibniz makes a parallel point for the rationalist argument. The upshot: if anyone commits a fallacy of composition, it is **Hume and Grayling**. From “each stick’s motion is explained by the next stick” it doesn’t follow that we’ve explained why there is any motion in the series at all; likewise for the image in the mirrors and the geometrical content of the books.

summary.heading: “Even if there were a first cause, why think it is God?”
summary.body:
Like “What caused God?”, this is often presented as devastating and is, Feser says, embarrassingly inept. Grayling refers offhandedly to the customary big leap from a first cause to the god of traditional religion; Dawkins says there is absolutely no reason to ascribe omnipotence, omniscience, and the like to a first cause; Krauss says much the same.

In fact defenders of every version of the argument have produced a great many arguments for the divine attributes. Aquinas spends around a hundred dense double-column pages of the *Summa Theologiae* (part I, right after the Five Ways) arguing that the cause of the world must be simple, good, infinite, immutable, one, knowing, living, willing, powerful, and so on; about two hundred pages of book 1 of the *Summa Contra Gentiles* cover the same ground; more appears in *De potentia* and *De veritate*. Much of Samuel Clarke’s *A Demonstration of the Being and Attributes of God* — as the title alone reveals — argues for infinity, omnipresence, unity, intelligence, free choice, power, wisdom, and goodness. Aristotle, Plotinus, Avicenna, Scotus, Leibniz, and recent defenders do likewise.

The New Atheists respond to none of these arguments and seem unaware they exist. And this book itself, in each of chapters 1–5 and at greater length in chapter 6, has argued that the first cause must be one, simple, immutable, eternal, immaterial, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good, and so forth. The claim that a successful First Cause argument wouldn’t reach the God of classical theism is groundless.

summary.heading: “It still wouldn’t prove prophets, the Bible, or the Trinity”
summary.body:
Feser’s reply: true, but completely irrelevant. The arguments never claimed to establish every doctrine of a particular religion — only one central tenet shared by many religions: that there is a cause of the world that is one, simple, immaterial, eternal, immutable, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good, and so on. If they succeed, atheism is false, and the remaining question is *which* form of theism to adopt — purely philosophical theism, Judaism, Christianity, Islam, or some other — a question requiring further investigation and argument.

It is silly to reason that because the arguments don’t answer every question about God they answer none. That would be like concluding that special relativity is false because it says nothing about whether and how living things evolved, or that quantum mechanics is wrong because it doesn’t answer every engineering question.

summary.heading: “The cosmological argument presupposes the ontological argument”
summary.body:
Kant famously raised this objection, and Grayling repeats it. Kant had Descartes’ ontological argument in mind: since existence is a perfection, a supremely perfect being that doesn’t exist is a contradiction, so such a being exists. If that argument worked, God would exist *by definition*, as a bachelor is unmarried by definition. The cosmological argument explains contingent things by a *necessary* being — so, Kant claims, it presupposes the ontological argument’s notion of necessity. But the ontological argument fails (existence, Kant says, is not a real perfection), so the cosmological argument falls with it.

**Reply, part one.** Aquinas and most Thomists explicitly reject the ontological argument while accepting the cosmological, so the critic must do more than assert a dependence. And there is no inconsistency in their position, as chapter 6 showed: when these arguments say God exists necessarily, they don’t mean he exists by definition. Definitional necessity is not the only kind, and it is not the kind they invoke. Kant’s objection would work only if it were.

**Grayling’s refinement.** Grayling allows that a defender might distinguish a *logically* necessary being (the ontological argument’s kind, which he finds dubious) from a *metaphysically* necessary being — one that must exist to serve as a stopping point for the regress, a ground for contingent existence. But he says this second notion is merely relative: it makes God a necessary *condition* of the world, not something that *could not have failed to exist*, which is what the argument needed.

**Reply, part two: a false dichotomy.** Metaphysical necessity can be spelled out without collapsing into either logical necessity or merely conditional necessity:

- For the **Aristotelian**, a thing is contingent because it mixes actuality and potentiality; what is purely actual, with no potentials that need or could be actualized, exists necessarily.
- For the **Neo-Platonist**, a thing is contingent because it is composite; what is absolutely simple has no parts that need or could be combined, and so is necessary.
- For the **Thomist**, the first cause is necessary because its essence simply *is* existence, so existence need not and cannot be added to it — and it is exactly that need which makes other things contingent.

Each of these gives God more than conditional necessity without making it the logical necessity of a proposition. A footnote sharpens the Thomist point: God’s essence *is* existence; it does not merely “include” existence, a common modern phrasing that suggests the very kind of composition Thomists and Neo-Platonists deny of God.

summary.heading: “God of the gaps”: the New Atheism’s central conceit
summary.body:
The objection: the cosmological argument posits God to plug a gap that science either already fills or eventually will. Feser calls this the central conceit of the whole New Atheist project: whatever can be explained will be explained scientifically, so “God” can at best be a quasi-scientific hypothesis — and a poor one. Hitchens says it violates Ockham’s razor. Dawkins says it is more economical to posit a Big Bang singularity or some physical concept not yet known. Harris says, more modestly, that nobody knows how or why the universe came to exist. Krauss, Hawking, and Mlodinow claim that science has already given (or nearly given) a complete non-theistic explanation — Hawking and Mlodinow asserting that because a law such as gravity exists, “the universe can and will create itself from nothing,” with Krauss devoting a whole book to the idea.

Feser identifies two basic problems. The **first** is that treating the existence of the universe as a question for empirical science rather than natural theology either misses the point or begs the question:

- **The proofs are not god-of-the-gaps arguments.** A god-of-the-gaps explanation allows that some non-divine explanation *could* in principle be right, and claims at most that the theistic one is more probable. The book’s arguments are attempts at *strict metaphysical demonstration*: they claim there is no possible way to account for their starting points except by a purely actual, absolutely simple, essence-is-existence, necessary cause. Right or wrong, they don’t stand or fall by the criteria used for empirical hypotheses — parsimony, fit with established theories, and the like.
- **Their starting points are metaphysical, not physical.** They concern what any empirical theory must presuppose. Whatever the empirical facts turn out to be, they will involve the actualization of potential (Aristotelian proof), composite things (Neo-Platonic), essences joined to existence (Thomistic), and contingency (rationalist). Declaring that only a scientific theory could count as a real explanation just assumes these arguments are mistaken; it doesn’t show it.

summary.heading: Krauss, Hawking, Mlodinow, and a “universe from nothing”
summary.body:
The **second** problem is that the proposed scientific explanation of the universe’s existence is plainly a nonstarter. A law like gravity is not *nothing*; so an account that appeals to such a law is obviously not an account of the universe arising from nothing.

Krauss’s book commits the same fallacy, and notoriously so — Feser notes that it was sharply criticized even by philosophers with no theological stake, most famously the philosopher of physics David Albert in a 2012 *New York Times* review. Over some 185 pages that promise to show how a universe can come from nothing, Krauss spends the first 152 arguing that it came from *empty space endowed with energy and governed by physical law* — which he admits is not nothing. By around page 170 he pares this back to *the laws of quantum gravity* — which he admits is not nothing either. At page 177 he falls back on the suggestion that there may simply be layer upon layer of laws.

What is never explained is how any of this shows the universe arising from nothing. There is ponderous talk of “candidates” for nothingness, of what nothing might “comprise”, of defining nothing on the basis of empirical evidence, and of nothing being as physical as something — as if nothingness were an unusually elusive kind of stuff that is hard to observe or measure. But nothing is not a stuff of any sort, not hard to define, doesn’t “comprise” anything, and isn’t mysterious: it is simply the absence of anything whatsoever. Krauss himself seems to know this, since he ends up conceding that his candidates aren’t really nothing. And what he is left with — a basic level of physical law, or layers of laws — is not only not nothing but, for the reasons given earlier, cannot be the ultimate explanation of the world.
